strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis showing that DiT block feature differences across timesteps follow a U-shaped redundancy pattern, providing intuition for the proposed caching strategy.

The proposed BWCache method is training-free and can be integrated as a plug-and-play component into multiple DiT-based video diffusion backbones (Open-Sora, Open-Sora-Plan, Latte) without architectural changes.

Extensive experimental evaluation across three base models, multiple video lengths/resolutions, and multi-GPU (DSP) scaling settings, with consistent speedups (up to ~2.24x, up to 17x with 8 GPUs) while maintaining competitive VBench/LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR scores relative to TeaCache and PAB.
Reasonably thorough ablations (threshold δ, reuse interval R, last-k steps) and a statistical significance test (paired t-test) supporting that quality differences vs. baselines are non-trivial.
Good set of qualitative comparisons (Figures 4, 7-10) across diverse prompts/styles that visually support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch between the title/motivation ("block-wise" caching implying block-granular reuse decisions) and the actual mechanism: the reuse trigger in Eq. (7) averages the relative L1 distance across all N blocks into a single global indicator, so the caching decision is applied uniformly to all blocks at a timestep rather than truly per-block, undermining the claimed advantage over coarse timestep-level caching methods like TeaCache.

Limited technical novelty: the core similarity indicator is a direct extension of TeaCache's relative-L1 reuse criterion (applied to blocks instead of raw inputs), and the periodic recomputation/progressive strategy is explicitly borrowed from PAB. The main contribution appears to be recombining existing ideas at a different granularity rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The comparison set omits several recent, directly relevant training-free caching baselines discussed in Related Work (e.g., AdaCache, DiTFastAttn, SmoothCache, FasterCache, ForwardCache/"Cache Me if You Can"), leaving open whether BWCache's advantages hold against the strongest recent competitors rather than only PAB/TeaCache/T-GATE/Δ-DiT.

Key hyperparameters (threshold δ, reuse interval R, last-k/2 cutoff) are manually preset per setting rather than learned or adaptively determined; the paper explicitly acknowledges this as a limitation deferred to future work, which limits the method's claimed generality across diverse generation tasks.

The method's benefit seems to partly stem from combining caching with a hand-tuned "never cache the last k/2 steps" heuristic, whose sensitivity and generality across models/tasks is not deeply analyzed beyond a single ablation table.

The paper lacks deeper theoretical or mechanistic justification for why per-block information (as opposed to timestep-level aggregate) yields meaningfully better reuse decisions, given that the actual decision rule is itself an aggregate statistic; the qualitative distinction from TeaCache is somewhat overstated in the text.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across five diverse DiT-based video generation models (Open-Sora, Open-Sora-Plan, Latte, Wan 2.1, HunyuanVideo), covering different architectures, samplers, and resolutions.

Comprehensive comparisons against a wide range of baselines (PAB, TeaCache, FasterCache, Skip-DiT, ProfilingDiT, TaylorSeer), including memory usage, multi-GPU scaling, and statistical significance (paired t-tests).
Thorough ablation studies on reuse rate, reuse interval, last-step recomputation, and block-subset selection for the cache indicator, providing practical guidance for parameter tuning.

The motivating analysis (U-shaped pattern of block feature variation across timesteps, latency breakdown showing DiT blocks dominate compute) is intuitive and well visualized, and is validated across multiple architectures.
Training-free and plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modification or retraining, which is practically appealing compared to methods like Skip-DiT.
Extensive appendix materials (dynamic scene evaluation, latent drift discussion, feature patterns in image/class-conditional generation) add depth and transparency about limitations.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: block-wise caching, L1-based similarity indicators, and periodic recomputation are each adaptations of existing ideas (e.g., PAB's progressive computation, TeaCache's relative L1 indicator, prior block-caching work for image diffusion such as Wimbauer et al. 2024), and the paper's core contribution is largely a recombination/re-tuning of these components at block-level granularity for video DiTs.
The similarity threshold δ is manually preset and requires per-model tuning (as acknowledged in the conclusion as future work), undermining the plug-and-play/training-free positioning to some extent.

The cache indicator computation itself is non-trivial, consuming 10.6%-22.5% of total inference time (Table 13), which is a substantial overhead that is not deeply optimized or justified against simpler alternatives.
On Open-Sora-Plan, TeaCache achieves notably higher speedup than BWCache (4.41x vs 2.24x in Table 1), and the explanation offered is somewhat post-hoc rather than a principled analysis.
Evaluation relies solely on automated metrics (VBench, LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR) without human perceptual studies, which is a known limitation for judging generative video quality.

The theoretical justification for the U-shaped redundancy pattern via frequency-domain analysis is asserted via a single citation without a rigorous derivation connecting it to the empirical observations.
The code link in the abstract appears to be a broken/placeholder text ('BetterBetterBetterBetter'), raising concerns about reproducibility at submission time.
